title: From a text file to a running program
summary: Create a real C++ source file, compile it with a real compiler, and see every stage between your text and an executable.

steps.title: Create a source file

checks.failMessage: There is no file called hello.cpp in projects/hello/ yet. Check the spelling and the folder.

hints: In VS Code: right-click the `hello` folder in the Explorer and choose **New File**. In a terminal: `touch hello.cpp` (macOS/Linux) or `ni hello.cpp` (PowerShell).
The file must be directly inside `projects/hello/`, not in a sub-folder.

steps.title: The smallest program

checks.label: hello.cpp defines int main()
checks.failMessage: The program needs a function called main that returns int: `int main() { ... }`.

checks.label: Program runs and exits with code 0

hints: A function is: return type, name, parameter list in `( )`, body in `{ }`.

steps.title: Say something
hints: `#include <iostream>` goes at the very top of the file, before `int main()`.
Capital H, capital C, a space, two plus signs. The checker ignores the trailing newline.

steps.title: Run the compiler yourself, one stage at a time
hints: Open a terminal **in the project folder** (`projects/hello`). In VS Code the C++ Studio panel has an *Open Terminal* button that does this.
Using clang? Replace `g++` with `clang++` — the flags are the same. On Windows with MSVC, see the table at the bottom of the step.

quiz.question: Your source file is about 7 lines, but hello.ii is tens of thousands of lines. Why?
options: The compiler adds debugging information to the file.
The preprocessor replaced `#include <iostream>` with the entire contents of the iostream header — and every header it includes.
hello.ii contains the machine code for your program.
The preprocessor copies the whole C++ standard library into every program.
explanations: Debug information is produced by the compiler (`-g`) and lives in the object file and executable, not in the preprocessed text.

Exactly. `#include` is textual copy-and-paste. The compiler proper never sees `#include` — it sees one enormous translation unit. This is why big projects care about include hygiene and build times, and one of the reasons C++20 introduced modules.
Machine code is produced later, by the compiler (into hello.o). hello.ii is still C++ source text — open it and look!
Close, but only the headers you include (and the headers *they* include) are pasted in — not the whole library. Most of the library's compiled code lives in a separate library the linker uses.

steps.title: Challenge: two lines

expect.equals:
Hello C++
I compiled this myself

hints: `\n` inside a string literal is a newline character.
You can chain: `std::cout << "first\n" << "second\n";` or use two separate statements.
